title: Influence of atmospheric moisture on the gas evolution tolerance of halide solid electrolytes
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
          <jats:p>Much attention has been paid on research and development on solid electrolytes for all-solid-state Li batteries. Although halide solid electrolytes such as Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>YCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> and Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>InCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> are promising due to fast Li ion conductivity and oxidation-resistant against positive electrode, a better understanding of their reactivity with atmospheric H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O is required for commercialization. In this study, the gas evolution tolerances of Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>YCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> and Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>InCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> were investigated. Temperature-programmed desorption mass spectrometry (TPD-MS) experiments at dew points below − 60 °C and gas detector tube experiments at dew points of − 30 °C both revealed significant differences in the H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O and HCl evolution behavior of Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>YCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> and Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>InCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub>. In TPD-MS, the onset temperature of HCl evolution for Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>YCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> (~ 100 °C) was significantly lower than that for Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>InCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> (~ 220 °C), indicating that Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>InCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> solid electrolytes have superior gas evolution tolerance. This difference may be attributable to differences in the retention of H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O derived from the material synthesis stage and from contact with the atmosphere during the measurements. In particular, based on first-principles calculations, the low-temperature HCl evolution observed in Li<jats:sub>3</jats:sub>YCl<jats:sub>6</jats:sub> was ascribed to the partial replacement of Cl<jats:sup>−</jats:sup> ions by OH<jats:sup>−</jats:sup> ions upon contamination with trace H<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>O. Because the heating and drying of solid electrolytes (including slurries) are inevitable processes during battery manufacturing, these findings can aid in the rational design of halide solid electrolytes for all-solid-state batteries.</jats:p>
